html:
The age when three rival kingdoms, Goguryeo, Baekje and Silla, shared the Korean peninsula and much of Manchuria, traditionally from 57 BCE to 668 CE. The traditional founding dates come from much later chronicles and are probably too early; the kingdoms took clear shape in the first centuries CE.

  • Goguryeo held the north of the peninsula, the Liaodong peninsula and much of Manchuria. It was the largest and fought both Chinese dynasties and steppe peoples.
  • Baekje held the southwest. It had close ties with Japan and passed on Chinese writing and Buddhism to the Yamato court.
  • Silla held the southeast and was at first the weakest.

Smaller states were swallowed along the way; the Gaya confederacy fell to Silla in 562.

All three shared a similar language and culture. Buddhism arrived in 372, when Goguryeo took it up, and became the faith of all three courts. Goguryeo beat back huge invasions by the Sui and then the Tang.

The end came through an alliance. Silla joined the Tang, and together they destroyed Baekje in 660 and Goguryeo in 668. Silla then fought its ally to keep the Tang out of the peninsula, and became Unified Silla. Refugees from Baekje fled to Japan, and Goguryeo's heirs later founded Balhae in the north. Korean identity grew from all three; the name Korea itself comes from Goguryeo through Goryeo.
